system.text:
You are the planning step of a defensive security triage system. You receive one network alert
raised by a machine-learning detector on a single flow record, plus the list of read-only tools an
investigator can call. Produce 2 to 6 short, concrete investigation questions that the tools can
answer, ordered by how much they would change the triage decision. Typical questions: whether the
source produced a burst of flows to many ports or hosts around the alert time; what the destination
asset is and how critical it is; whether the source is a known attacker or an internal host; whether
a vulnerability or an ATT&CK technique matches the observed pattern; whether neighbouring flows
also score as attacks. Do not answer the questions yourself. Respond only with the JSON object.

content.text: {"questions":["How many flows did 172.16.0.1 send to 192.168.10.50 on port 21 within ±30 minutes of event 1110604, and do they show a high-rate pattern of short connections ending in resets that fits repeated login attempts?","What is 192.168.10.50 in the asset inventory (hostname, role, OS, whether it runs an FTP service) and how critical is it?","Is 172.16.0.1 a known attacker address or a firewall/NAT gateway, and which network zone does it belong to?","Do neighbouring flows from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:21 also score above the detector threshold as brute_force?","Did 172.16.0.1 also contact other ports or hosts around the alert time (for example SSH on 22), which would point to a wider credential-guessing or scanning campaign?","Does MITRE ATT&CK T1110 (Brute Force) match the observed pattern, and are there known FTP vulnerabilities for the service that the asset record identifies?"],"rationale":"The detector flags an FTP (port 21) flow as brute_force with very high confidence, driven by small backward packets and RST flags. The most decisive check is whether this is one of many repeated short sessions on the same source-destination pair, which would confirm password guessing. Next come how critical the target is and whether it actually runs FTP, then the reputation of the source. 172.16.0.1 may be a firewall or NAT address that masks an external attacker. Rescoring neighbouring flows, checking how broad the source's activity is, and mapping to ATT&CK or a CVE would support scoping and the write-up."}
